subtype: Approach: three-account structure of joint and personal money [Action]
passage: Rehana, you asked how my husband and I avoid fights about money. I'm Gurleen. When we married, we set up three accounts. One joint account for rent, bills and groceries. Each of us put in a share that matched our income, not half and half: he earned more then, so he put in more. And two personal accounts, for anything we liked, with no explaining. My first buy from mine was a set of oil paints I'd never have justified to anyone. That is what I mean: safe together, free apart. It wasn't perfect, and we adjusted the shares when my income grew. But it saved us from a great many arguments, and neither of us ever felt watched.

qa.q: What goes into the joint account?
qa.a: The joint account is for rent, bills and groceries.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel about the personal account?
qa.a: Gurleen felt free and pleased, buying oil paints with no need to justify it.

qa.q: Which choice in the story kept the arrangement fair, and why?
qa.a: Putting in a share matching each income, not half and half, kept it fair, because each person's contribution fitted what they earned.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's husband have seen the shares matching income?
qa.a: He probably saw it as fair and steady, since he put in more when he earned more and the shares changed when Gurleen's income grew.

grounding: Illustrates a couple with a joint account for rent and bills funded in proportion to income, plus separate personal accounts, giving shared security and individual freedom.

subtype: Approach: three-account structure of joint and personal money [Action]
passage:
The bank branch near Sangeeta's office in Indore closed at three on Saturdays, and she and her husband, Mohit, had exactly one lunch hour to set things up.
They'd worked it out the night before. One joint account for rent, electricity and groceries. Each would put in a share matched to their salary: Mohit earned more, so he'd put in more. Whatever was left stayed in their own separate accounts, no questions asked.
At the counter, Disha, the account officer, handed them forms. "Joint account, either can operate?"
"Yes," Sangeeta said. "And the standing instructions from both salaries on the first."
The queue behind them grew. Mohit's pen ran out. Disha lent him hers.
At two forty-five they walked out with the passbook. Sangeeta laughed. "Now if I buy another plant, you can't say a word."
"And my cricket kit is none of your business," Mohit said.

qa.q: When did the bank branch close on Saturdays?
How did Sangeeta and Mohit seem to feel walking out of the bank?
qa.a: They felt relieved and light-hearted, joking about plants and a cricket kit because personal spending was now their own.

qa.q: What else could Sangeeta and Mohit do to keep the arrangement fair over time?
qa.a: They could review the shares together if either salary changes, so the joint account still feels proportional.

qa.q: How does the setup look from Mohit's side?
qa.a: Mohit pays a bigger share into the joint account, which feels fair given his salary, while he keeps freedom over his own money.

grounding: It shows a couple opening a joint account for rent and bills with contributions matched to income, while keeping separate accounts for personal spending.

subtype: Approach: three-account structure of joint and personal money [Action]
passage:
Yash and Pallavi had been married four months when they sat down in their Andheri flat with a notebook and Sahil, Yash's old college friend who worked at a bank, on a video call.
"We don't want to fight about every coffee," Pallavi said.
Sahil explained what he'd seen other couples do. Yash and Pallavi decided their own version. One joint account for rent, bills and groceries. Pallavi earned more, so she would put in a bigger share; they agreed on proportions that matched their salaries. Everything else would stay in their own accounts.
On Monday they opened the joint account and set up transfers for the first of each month.
Three weeks later, Yash bought an expensive pair of running shoes. Pallavi raised an eyebrow, then shrugged. "Your account, your shoes."
Yash grinned. "Your account, your pottery classes."

qa.q: When were the transfers set up for?
How did Pallavi feel when Yash bought the running shoes?
qa.a: She was briefly surprised, then relaxed, shrugging because personal spending was Yash's own choice under their arrangement.

qa.q: What else could Yash and Pallavi do if the joint account ran short one month?
qa.a: They could talk it through together and adjust the proportions or bills, and ask a qualified adviser if they're unsure of the options.

qa.q: How does the arrangement look from Yash's side?
qa.a: Yash feels free to spend personal money without questions, while knowing the shared bills are covered.

grounding: It shows a couple opening a joint account for rent and bills with contributions matched to income and keeping separate personal accounts.
